subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Asexual copies the parent; sexual mixes new combinations
The menstrual cycle and its hormones
What happens at fertilization in humans
Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
Puberty starts in the hypothalamus
Making sperm and making eggs
The placenta supplies the foetus without mixing bloods
Progesterone keeps pregnancy going; its fall lets birth begin
Phenotypic plasticity: adjusting without changing genes
PKU: a recessive condition
Haemophilia is X-linked
Continuous variation, polygenes and averages
Dihybrid ratios: 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1
Linked genes travel together
What homeostasis keeps steady
Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
The human responses to hot and cold
Excretion and osmoregulation are different jobs
The loop of Henle salts the medulla
Blood is redirected as activity changes

questions.q: Aphids reproduce asexually through the summer, when conditions are stable and food is plentiful, and switch to sexual reproduction in autumn before conditions change. Which statement best explains this pattern?
options: Sexual reproduction is used in autumn because varied offspring are invariably fitter; the summer clones are a poor substitute produced under time pressure.
Summer clones copy an adapted genotype quickly; autumn sexual reproduction produces varied offspring for the changed conditions ahead.
Sexual reproduction is used in autumn so that the offspring gain the specific cold-tolerance features that the coming winter demands.
Asexual reproduction in summer shows that aphids are simple organisms; the autumn sexual stage is their true form of reproduction.
optionWhy: A student who believes variation is always an advantage picks this. In stable summer conditions the clones are the better strategy: every offspring inherits the whole adapted genotype.

Asexual reproduction suits an individual already adapted to the existing environment, giving many identical offspring fast. Sexual reproduction produces new gene combinations, the variation needed for adaptation to a changed environment.
A student who thinks variation is directed towards what is needed picks this. New allele combinations are random; some may happen to suit winter, and selection then favours those.

A student who files asexual reproduction with bacteria and simple organisms picks this. Many eukaryotes, including these insects, use both modes; the choice depends on the environment, not on complexity.
questions.explain: Asexual reproduction suits an individual already adapted to the existing environment, giving many identical offspring fast. Sexual reproduction produces new gene combinations, the variation needed for adaptation to a changed environment.

questions.q: Blood samples were taken from a woman on day 7 and day 21 of a regular 28-day cycle. Progesterone was very low on day 7 and high on day 21. What can be concluded about day 21?
options: A corpus luteum has formed after ovulation and is secreting progesterone that maintains the endometrium.
The pituitary gland has increased its progesterone output in preparation for menstruation.
Ovulation is about to occur, because the egg is released when menstruation begins on day 28.
The rising progesterone will itself trigger the menstruation that is due on day 28.
optionWhy: High progesterone a week after mid-cycle shows that ovulation has occurred and the ruptured follicle has become a corpus luteum, whose progesterone keeps the thickened endometrium in place.
A student who assigns progesterone to the pituitary picks this. Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum in the ovary, and it postpones menstruation rather than preparing for it.
A student who links egg release to menstruation picks this. Ovulation occurred around day 14; the high progesterone is evidence that it has already happened.
A student who expects a rise to cause the event picks this. Menstruation follows the fall in progesterone when the corpus luteum degenerates.
questions.explain: High progesterone a week after mid-cycle shows that ovulation has occurred and the ruptured follicle has become a corpus luteum, whose progesterone keeps the thickened endometrium in place.

questions.q: A mutation in mitochondrial DNA is passed from a mother to all her children but is never passed on by a father. Which feature of fertilization explains this?
options: Sperm mitochondria enter the egg but are so outnumbered by the egg's own that their DNA is diluted away.
Each parent hands over exactly half of its DNA, and the mitochondrial DNA happens to fall in the mother's half.
The egg is larger because it carries more genetic material, including all the mitochondria required.
The sperm's mitochondria are destroyed after its nucleus has entered the egg cytoplasm.
optionWhy: A student who believes the sperm's mitochondria get in picks this. They do not enter: they are destroyed with the tail, so no paternal mitochondrial DNA is present to be diluted.

A student who pictures inheritance as each parent handing over a fixed half of its DNA picks this. Meiosis halves the nuclear DNA only; mitochondrial DNA is not part of that division, and the father passes on none because the sperm's mitochondria are destroyed at fertilization.

A student who equates the egg's size with extra genetic material picks this. The egg's size is due to food reserves; maternal inheritance of mitochondria is due to the fate of the sperm's mitochondria.
Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed. All the zygote's mitochondria, and so all its mitochondrial DNA, come from the egg.
questions.explain: Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg; the sperm's tail and mitochondria are destroyed. All the zygote's mitochondria, and so all its mitochondrial DNA, come from the egg.

questions.q: Garden pea flowers pollinate and fertilize themselves before they open. Which statement about reproduction in the pea is correct?
options: It is asexual, because only one parent plant takes part in the process.
Fertilization is complete as soon as the pollen has landed on the flower's stigma.
It is sexual, because meiosis makes the gametes and they fuse at fertilization.
The pollen grains, being the male gametes, fuse directly with the ovules in the ovary.
optionWhy: A student who defines asexual reproduction by the number of parents picks this. The pea's gametes are made by meiosis and fuse, so its reproduction is sexual even though it self-fertilizes.
A student who equates pollination with fertilization picks this. After pollination a pollen tube must grow down the style before a male gamete can fuse with the female gamete.

Reproduction in flowering plants is sexual even if a plant is hermaphroditic: gametes formed by meiosis fuse to give a zygote. Whether the offspring differ from the parent depends on how heterozygous it is; what makes the process sexual is meiosis and fusion of gametes, not the number of parents.
A student who treats pollen as the gamete picks this. The pollen grain grows a tube that delivers the male gametes it contains to the female gamete inside the ovule.
questions.explain: Reproduction in flowering plants is sexual even if a plant is hermaphroditic: gametes formed by meiosis fuse to give a zygote. Whether the offspring differ from the parent depends on how heterozygous it is; what makes the process sexual is meiosis and fusion of gametes, not the number of parents.

questions.q: A child whose hypothalamus cannot release GnRH fails to enter puberty, although the pituitary gland and gonads are normal. Which explanation is correct?
options: GnRH normally acts directly on the gonads, so without it they cannot make sex hormones; the pituitary gland plays no part in puberty.
Without GnRH the pituitary does not increase LH and FSH release, so the gonads are not stimulated to raise sex hormone production.
The gonads should start puberty on their own, so the fault must in fact lie in the testes or the ovaries themselves.
Puberty requires the pituitary gland to secrete the steroid sex hormones, which it cannot do without GnRH.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'gonadotropin' as 'acts on gonads' picks this. GnRH acts on the pituitary, which releases the gonadotropins LH and FSH that act on the gonads.

Puberty is triggered by increased GnRH release from the hypothalamus, which raises LH and FSH secretion by the pituitary; these stimulate the gonads to secrete the sex hormones that cause the changes of puberty.
A student who places the origin of puberty in the gonads picks this. Normal gonads stay inactive without LH and FSH, which in turn depend on GnRH.
A student who thinks the pituitary makes steroid hormones picks this. The pituitary secretes LH and FSH; testosterone, oestradiol and progesterone are made by the gonads.
questions.explain: Puberty is triggered by increased GnRH release from the hypothalamus, which raises LH and FSH secretion by the pituitary; these stimulate the gonads to secrete the sex hormones that cause the changes of puberty.

questions.q: A man produces about 100 million sperm per day. A woman is born with about a million egg-forming cells arrested in meiosis, and releases only about 400 eggs in her lifetime. Which conclusion do these figures best support?
options: Eggs are produced continuously like sperm, but nearly all are broken down before they can be ovulated.
Each of the million cells produced four eggs, most of which were not released from the ovary.
The sperm figure must be an overestimate, since fertilization needs only one sperm for each egg.
Egg-forming cells are all made before birth and are then used sparingly over a lifetime.
optionWhy: A student who assumes continuous production picks this. The figures show a fixed stock formed before birth; most of those cells degenerate, but none are newly made after birth.
A student who applies the four-products rule picks this. Each cell that completes meiosis yields one egg plus polar bodies, so four million eggs were never present.
A student who expects gamete numbers to match picks this. Vast sperm numbers are the norm because so few survive the journey to the egg.

Oogenesis begins in the foetus with mitosis, growth and the start of meiosis; from puberty a few cells resume meiosis each cycle and one egg is usually released, whereas spermatogenesis produces millions of new sperm daily.
questions.explain: Oogenesis begins in the foetus with mitosis, growth and the start of meiosis; from puberty a few cells resume meiosis each cycle and one egg is usually released, whereas spermatogenesis produces millions of new sperm daily.

questions.q: A foetus in the uterus has fluid-filled, collapsed lungs, yet its blood is oxygenated. How does oxygen reach the blood of the foetus?
options: Maternal blood carrying oxygen flows through the placenta into the blood vessels of the foetus.
The placenta filters oxygen out of the mother's blood while blocking all harmful substances.
The foetus breathes it in from the surrounding amniotic fluid, using its own lungs.
It diffuses from maternal blood into foetal capillaries in the placental villi.
optionWhy: A student who imagines a shared circulation picks this. Maternal and foetal blood stay separate; oxygen crosses from one to the other in the villi.
A student who sees the placenta as a selective filter picks this. Exchange is by diffusion and transport according to physical properties, and some harmful substances cross.
A student who knows no route to oxygen other than breathing picks this. The foetal lungs are fluid-filled and unused; all gas exchange is across the placenta.
Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient from maternal blood in the placenta into foetal blood in the capillaries of the villi, whose large surface area makes exchange rapid.
questions.explain: Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient from maternal blood in the placenta into foetal blood in the capillaries of the villi, whose large surface area makes exchange rapid.

questions.q: In a mammal, removing the ovaries (and with them the corpus luteum) early in pregnancy ended the pregnancy, but the same operation late in pregnancy did not. What does this show?
options: The placenta maintained the pregnancy in both cases; the early loss was caused by the stress of surgery.
Later in pregnancy the mother's pituitary gland takes over progesterone secretion, so the ovaries are no longer needed.
Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum at first and later by the placenta once it has formed.
Late in pregnancy the mother's pituitary secretes hCG, which replaced the missing progesterone.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the placenta works from implantation picks this. Early on there is no functioning placenta; the corpus luteum is the only source of the progesterone needed.
A student who places progesterone in the pituitary picks this. Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta; the pituitary secretes FSH, LH and oxytocin, not progesterone.
Continuity of pregnancy depends on progesterone, secreted initially by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta. Once the placenta has taken over, the ovaries are no longer needed.
A student who assigns hCG to a maternal gland picks this. hCG is made by the embryo and placenta, and it is placental progesterone, not hCG, that sustains late pregnancy.
questions.explain: Continuity of pregnancy depends on progesterone, secreted initially by the corpus luteum and then by the placenta. Once the placenta has taken over, the ovaries are no longer needed.

questions.q: A person's skin darkens after several weeks in strong sunlight and returns to its previous colour over the winter. How is this change best explained?
options: It is phenotypic plasticity: ultraviolet light causes mutations in the melanin genes, which produce extra pigment until the mutations are repaired in winter
Phenotypic plasticity: sunlight alters the expression of genes for melanin production, and the change reverses because the genotype is unchanged
It is an adaptation acquired during life, and because it is adaptive it will be permanent and passed on to the person's children
It is a trait due to environment only, so it forms no part of the person's phenotype and involves no change in gene expression
optionWhy: A student who thinks a new trait needs a change in the genes picks this. Phenotypic plasticity is not due to changes in genotype; the base sequences of the alleles are unaltered and only their expression changes.

Phenotypic plasticity is the capacity to develop traits suited to the environment experienced by varying patterns of gene expression. The alleles are exactly as inherited, so when the environmental signal is removed the expression pattern, and the trait, can revert.

A student who applies the evolutionary sense of adaptation to an individual picks this. The stem itself shows the change reverses, and since the genotype is unchanged the tan cannot be inherited by offspring.

A student who thinks only inherited traits count as phenotype picks this. Phenotype includes all observable traits however they arise, and a tan is produced by increased expression of the genes for melanin synthesis in response to light.
questions.explain: Phenotypic plasticity is the capacity to develop traits suited to the environment experienced by varying patterns of gene expression. The alleles are exactly as inherited, so when the environmental signal is removed the expression pattern, and the trait, can revert.

questions.q: A man and a woman are both unaffected carriers of the PKU allele. They already have one child with PKU. What is the probability that their next child will have PKU?
optionWhy: A student who treats the 2 in 4 heterozygous carriers as the children who 'have' PKU picks this. Carriers are unaffected, because one functional allele produces enough enzyme; only the 1 in 4 homozygous recessive (pp) children have PKU.

A student who believes PKU is caused by a dominant allele expects three quarters of the children of two heterozygotes to be affected. PKU is recessive, so only the homozygous recessive quarter is affected.

A student who reads a 3:1 ratio as a quota picks this, thinking the family has already had its one affected child in four. Each fertilization is independent; the probability is 1 in 4 for every child regardless of earlier children.

Both parents are heterozygous (Pp × Pp). The Punnett grid gives PP, Pp, pP and pp, so each fertilization has a 1 in 4 chance of producing a homozygous recessive child with PKU. Each child is an independent event, so the earlier affected child makes no difference.
questions.explain: Both parents are heterozygous (Pp × Pp). The Punnett grid gives PP, Pp, pP and pp, so each fertilization has a 1 in 4 chance of producing a homozygous recessive child with PKU. Each child is an independent event, so the earlier affected child makes no difference.

questions.q: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia (XHXh) has children with a man who does not have haemophilia (XHY). Their first child is a boy. What is the probability that he has haemophilia?
optionWhy: A student who takes the 1 in 4 from the whole Punnett grid (XHXH, XHXh, XHY, XhY) and applies it to a son picks this. Among sons only, the two possibilities are XHY and XhY, so the probability is 1 in 2.
A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X from his mother. The mother passes XH or Xh with equal probability, so half of sons on average are XhY and have haemophilia.

A student who believes a carrier mother passes the condition to all of her sons picks this. She has one XH and one Xh and passes either with equal probability, so only half of her sons are expected to be affected.

A student who thinks haemophilia passes from father to son, and notes that this father is unaffected, picks this. A son inherits his X chromosome from his mother, so a carrier mother can have affected sons whatever the father's genotype.
questions.explain: A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X from his mother. The mother passes XH or Xh with equal probability, so half of sons on average are XhY and have haemophilia.

questions.q: The heights in centimetres of nine students are: 150, 152, 152, 155, 158, 160, 163, 170 and 175. What are the mean, median and mode of these heights?
options: Mean 158 cm, median 159.4 cm, and mode 152 cm
Mean of 159.4 cm, median 152 cm, mode 158 cm
Mean 158.6 cm, with median 158 cm and mode 152 cm
Mean 159.4 cm, median 158 cm, mode 152 cm
optionWhy: A student who thinks the median is the calculated average and the mean is the middle value swaps the two. The mean is the sum divided by the number of values, 159.4; the median is the middle value in order, 158.

A student who takes the mode to be the middle value and the median to be the most frequent value swaps those two. The median is the middle value, 158; the mode is the value that occurs most often, 152.

A student who treats the highest and lowest values as outliers and discards both before calculating picks this: (1435 − 175 − 150) / 7 = 158.6. A value is an outlier only if it lies more than 1.5 × IQR beyond a quartile; by that rule none of these nine values is an outlier, and the mean of the full data set is 159.4 cm.

The nine values sum to 1435, and 1435 / 9 = 159.4 (to one decimal place). The values are already in order, so the median is the fifth value, 158. The only value that appears twice is 152, so it is the mode.
questions.explain: The nine values sum to 1435, and 1435 / 9 = 159.4 (to one decimal place). The values are already in order, so the median is the fifth value, 158. The only value that appears twice is 152, so it is the mode.

questions.q: Mendel's second law predicts a 9:3:3:1 ratio in the F2 of a dihybrid cross, yet a cross involving two genes close together on the same chromosome gives a ratio far from this. What does this show about the law?
options: The law is universal, so the unexpected ratio must be the result of new mutations or of errors made in scoring the offspring
The law still applies because all genes assort independently; the unexpected ratio must arise from unequal survival of the different offspring
The law applies only to autosomal genes, so this deviation shows that the two genes must be located on one of the two sex chromosomes
The law applies only when genes are on different chromosomes or far enough apart to recombine freely; all biological laws have exceptions
optionWhy: A student who has learned the law without its conditions picks this. The deviation is real and repeatable: genes close together on one chromosome are inherited together, and no scoring error or mutation is needed to explain it.

A student who believes every gene assorts independently picks this. Genes on the same chromosome do not assort independently, because their alleles travel together unless crossing over separates them, so the ratio changes with no difference in survival.

A student who equates linkage with sex linkage picks this. Two genes close together on any chromosome, including an autosome, are linked; the stem says nothing about sex chromosomes, and autosomal linkage is the common case.

Mendel's second law applies only if genes are on different chromosomes or are far enough apart on one chromosome for recombination rates to reach 50%. Linked genes are a genuine exception, and students should recognize that there are exceptions to all biological laws under certain conditions.
questions.explain: Mendel's second law applies only if genes are on different chromosomes or are far enough apart on one chromosome for recombination rates to reach 50%. Linked genes are a genuine exception, and students should recognize that there are exceptions to all biological laws under certain conditions.

questions.q: In a fruit fly the loci for body colour and wing shape are on the same autosome. A fly inherited one chromosome carrying the alleles G and W and the homologous chromosome carrying g and w, shown as G W and g w beside two vertical lines. Why does this fly not produce GW, Gw, gW and gw gametes in equal numbers?
options: The two genes are permanently joined together on the chromosome, so only GW and gw gametes can ever be formed by this fly
The alleles on each chromosome are passed on together unless crossing over between the loci separates them, which occurs in only some meioses
Because the genes are linked they must be on the X chromosome, so only female flies are able to produce the recombinant gametes
Because the fly received G and W from one parent and g and w from the other, the alleles from each parent stay together as a set in its gametes
optionWhy: A student who takes 'linked' to mean inseparable picks this. Crossing over between the loci exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids, so recombinant Gw and gW gametes are produced, though at less than 50%.

Linked alleles fail to assort independently because they are on the same DNA molecule. GW and gw gametes are the majority; Gw and gW recombinant gametes arise only when a chiasma forms between the two loci in prophase I, and the closer the loci the less often that happens.
A student who equates linkage with sex linkage picks this. The stem states the loci are on an autosome; autosomal linkage has nothing to do with the sex chromosomes or the sex of the fly.

A student who thinks alleles from the same parent travel as a set picks this. Alleles stay together here because the two loci are on the same chromosome, not because of their parental origin; for unlinked genes the parental combinations are broken up by independent assortment, and even for linked genes crossing over produces some recombinants.
questions.explain: Linked alleles fail to assort independently because they are on the same DNA molecule. GW and gw gametes are the majority; Gw and gW recombinant gametes arise only when a chiasma forms between the two loci in prophase I, and the closer the loci the less often that happens.

questions.q: A person's core temperature was recorded at intervals through a day on which the air temperature ranged from 5 °C to 30 °C. The readings were 36.6, 36.9, 37.2, 36.8 and 37.1 °C. What do these readings show?
options: Homeostasis has failed, because the core temperature was not held at one constant value through the day.
Core temperature is being kept within preset limits despite large changes in the external environment.
The readings cannot show homeostasis: skin temperature, not the core, is what is kept within limits.
Only the readings above 37 °C were brought back by negative feedback; the lower ones were not.
optionWhy: A student who expects a homeostatic variable to be perfectly constant picks this. Small oscillations around the set point are the normal signature of negative feedback, not evidence of failure.

The air temperature varied by 25 °C but the core temperature stayed within 0.4 °C of 37 °C (a total range of only 0.6 °C). That is homeostasis: the internal variable fluctuates only within narrow preset limits while the external environment changes far more.

A student who takes the regulated variable to be the body's surface rather than its internal environment picks this. Skin temperature is allowed to vary widely; it is the core temperature, along with blood pH, blood glucose and blood osmotic concentration, that is held within preset limits (D3.3.1).

A student who thinks negative feedback corrects only rises picks this. The readings below 37 °C were also followed by a return towards the set point, because negative feedback acts from both directions.
questions.explain: The air temperature varied by 25 °C but the core temperature stayed within 0.4 °C of 37 °C (a total range of only 0.6 °C). That is homeostasis: the internal variable fluctuates only within narrow preset limits while the external environment changes far more.

questions.q: A lean 12-year-old develops very high blood glucose within a few weeks; antibodies against pancreatic islet cells are found in the blood and blood insulin is very low. A 55-year-old with obesity has had slowly rising fasting blood glucose for years, with a high blood insulin concentration. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: The child has type 1 diabetes from autoimmune loss of beta cells; the adult has type 2, with insulin secreted but target cells resistant to it.
Both have the same disorder, a pancreas that has stopped making insulin, seen at an early and at a late stage of the disease.
The child's diabetes must have been caused by a sugary diet, because it appeared in childhood; the adult's by the ageing of the pancreas.
Both need insulin injections at once, because a high blood glucose concentration shows that insulin is lacking in each case.
optionWhy: Islet-cell antibodies, rapid onset in childhood and very low insulin point to autoimmune destruction of beta cells (type 1). Years of rising glucose despite high insulin, with obesity, show that insulin is present but its targets are not responding (type 2 insulin resistance).
A student who believes all diabetes is an insulin shortage picks this. The adult's blood insulin is high, which rules out a failure to make insulin; the problem is the response of the target cells.
A student who transfers the lifestyle explanation of type 2 onto type 1 picks this. The islet-cell antibodies show an autoimmune cause in the child; diet does not cause type 1 and cannot prevent it.

A student who equates diabetes treatment with insulin injection picks this. The child does need insulin. The adult has plenty of insulin already; the first treatments are weight loss, diet and exercise to restore sensitivity, with drugs added if needed.
questions.explain: Islet-cell antibodies, rapid onset in childhood and very low insulin point to autoimmune destruction of beta cells (type 1). Years of rising glucose despite high insulin, with obesity, show that insulin is present but its targets are not responding (type 2 insulin resistance).

questions.q: Brown adipose tissue in a newborn baby releases heat when the baby is cold. Which statement describes the mechanism?
options: The mitochondria make ATP unusually fast, and the ATP is then broken down to release heat.
The tissue forms a thick insulating layer of fat, so heat generated elsewhere in the body is retained.
Protons re-enter the mitochondrial matrix without passing through ATP synthase, releasing heat.
Thyroxin from the hypothalamus stimulates the tissue, raising its metabolic rate within seconds.
optionWhy: A student who cannot picture respiration without ATP as its product picks this. In uncoupled respiration ATP synthase is bypassed; the heat is released directly from the dissipation of the proton gradient, not from ATP hydrolysis.
A student who thinks all fat is insulation picks this. That is the role of white adipose tissue; brown adipose tissue is an active heat generator packed with mitochondria.

An uncoupling protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose cells lets protons flow back into the matrix without driving ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient built by the electron transport chain is released as heat rather than stored in ATP. This is uncoupled respiration.

A student who attaches thyroxin to the wrong gland and the wrong time scale picks this. Thyroxin is secreted by the thyroid gland and changes heat production over days; brown adipose tissue in a cold baby is activated by sympathetic nerve impulses and generates heat by uncoupled respiration in its mitochondria (D3.3.6).
questions.explain: An uncoupling protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose cells lets protons flow back into the matrix without driving ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient built by the electron transport chain is released as heat rather than stored in ATP. This is uncoupled respiration.

questions.q: Blood plasma has an osmotic concentration of about 0.30 osmol L−1. Red blood cells are placed in a 0.15 mol L−1 solution of sodium chloride, which dissociates fully into ions. What happens to the cells?
options: Nothing visible: the solution is 0.30 osmol L−1, the same as plasma, so there is no net osmosis.
The cells swell, because 0.15 osmol L−1 is half the osmotic concentration of the plasma.
The cells shrink, as water leaves them for the more dilute 0.15 osmol L−1 solution outside.
The cells shrink, because water moves to where there is more water, and the saline has more.
optionWhy: Each mole of NaCl gives two moles of osmotically active particles, so 0.15 mol L−1 NaCl is 0.30 osmol L−1. That equals the osmotic concentration of plasma, so water enters and leaves the cells at equal rates. This is why 0.15 mol L−1 (0.9%) saline is used clinically.
A student who equates osmotic concentration with molar concentration picks this. NaCl dissociates into two ions per formula unit, so the osmotic concentration is 0.30 osmol L−1, not 0.15.

A student who thinks water moves towards the more dilute solution, and who has also ignored dissociation, picks this. Water moves towards higher osmotic concentration, and in any case the solution is 0.30 osmol L−1, equal to plasma.

A student who thinks water moves towards the more dilute side picks this. Osmosis is net movement of water from lower to higher osmotic concentration; here the saline is 0.30 osmol L−1 once its ions are counted, equal to the cell contents and the plasma, so there is no net movement (D3.3.7).
questions.explain: Each mole of NaCl gives two moles of osmotically active particles, so 0.15 mol L−1 NaCl is 0.30 osmol L−1. That equals the osmotic concentration of plasma, so water enters and leaves the cells at equal rates. This is why 0.15 mol L−1 (0.9%) saline is used clinically.

questions.q: In a healthy kidney the osmotic concentration of the interstitial fluid rises from 0.3 osmol L−1 in the cortex to about 1.2 osmol L−1 in the deep medulla. A drug blocks the active transport of sodium ions in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Which prediction is best supported?
options: The medullary gradient decays towards 0.3 osmol L−1, so less water leaves the collecting ducts and the urine becomes more dilute.
The loop can no longer reabsorb water directly, but the collecting ducts are unaffected, so the urine is unchanged.
Water reabsorption in the collecting ducts continues normally, because it is driven by pumps that ADH switches on.
Urea can no longer be excreted, so it accumulates in the blood while the volume of urine stays about the same.
optionWhy: The high osmotic concentration of the medulla is maintained by sodium ions pumped out of the ascending limb. Without that pumping the gradient dissipates, the osmotic force drawing water out of the collecting ducts weakens, and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced (this is how loop diuretics act).

A student who thinks the loop's job is to remove water itself picks this. The loop's contribution is the medullary gradient; losing it does affect the collecting ducts, because there is no longer a strong osmotic gradient to draw water out of them.

A student who believes ADH activates water pumps picks this. ADH only inserts aquaporins; the driving force is osmosis into the concentrated medulla. With the gradient gone, aquaporins alone cannot move much water.

A student who merges osmoregulation with excretion picks this. Urea is removed by filtration and left in the filtrate; blocking sodium transport in the loop changes water balance, not the excretion of urea.
questions.explain: The high osmotic concentration of the medulla is maintained by sodium ions pumped out of the ascending limb. Without that pumping the gradient dissipates, the osmotic force drawing water out of the collecting ducts weakens, and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced (this is how loop diuretics act).

questions.q: During sleep, cardiac output falls to about 4 dm3 per minute. Which pattern of blood supply to the organs is expected?
options: Muscle flow is minimal and brain flow is maintained, while the gut and kidneys still receive large shares.
Every organ's blood flow falls by the same fraction, because the heart is simply pumping less blood.
Brain blood flow falls to a small fraction of its waking value, since the brain itself is resting.
Kidney blood flow falls to near zero, since so little metabolic waste is produced during sleep.
optionWhy: With no muscular work, skeletal muscle arterioles are constricted and muscle takes little of the output. The brain's flow is held nearly constant in all states. The gut and kidneys, no longer competing with muscle, continue to receive large shares for digestion and excretion.

A student who thinks cardiac output is shared out in fixed proportions picks this. Arterioles in each organ set its share, so a fall in output is not spread evenly: muscle loses most, the brain loses almost nothing.

A student who assumes brain blood flow tracks how busy the brain feels picks this. Brain flow is kept nearly constant during sleep, wakeful rest and exercise alike; the sleeping brain remains highly active.

A student who reasons from imagined need picks this. Metabolism, and so urea production, continues during sleep, and the kidneys keep receiving a large share of cardiac output; it is during vigorous exercise that their flow is cut.
questions.explain: With no muscular work, skeletal muscle arterioles are constricted and muscle takes little of the output. The brain's flow is held nearly constant in all states. The gut and kidneys, no longer competing with muscle, continue to receive large shares for digestion and excretion.
